name: Greyish Brown
lede: Greyish brown is a plain descriptive name for a muted, earthy brown, and it is one of the most common colors in the paintings we have measured.

sections.title: A plain description
sections.body:
Greyish brown is a description rather than a named thing: a brown with grey in it, a dull, low-chroma tone [1]. It first shows up in our sources in the 1955 ISCC-NBS list and later in the xkcd survey of 2010 [2]. Older dictionaries use the same two words to define other names instead. A dun is greyish-brown and dingy, beaver is the greyish brown of beaver fur, a deer-coloured thing has a tawny-red or greyish-brown hide, and clove brown is a greyish brown [1].

So the phrase works as a bridge between a [[brown]] and a [[grey]], and the books reach for it whenever they need to describe a natural, undyed color.

sections.title: The color of undyed things
sections.body:
Paterson lists greyish browns among the colors of undyed cloth, earth, stone and wood, together with light browns, off-whites and greys [1]. Medieval linen shows the same drift: laundry-bleached white was hard to keep white, and the cloth turned grayish brown, yellow or ecru as time passed [3][4]. A grayish brown ground was also found on an Egyptian mummy case lid, a layer containing lime spar and quartz [5].

Birren repeats an old claim that a grayish brown means selfishness [6]. That is a historic opinion and not modern evidence; colors do not carry fixed meanings [6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Greyish brown appears in 22.25% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, 5,291 paintings, as photographed, which makes it more common than 99% of the named colors [7]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 29% of the 3,269 paintings where we measure roles [7].

It peaks in the 1100s, where 23 of the 50 paintings we hold from then contain it, 2.1x the baseline of the same museums [7]. That century is thin in the archive, and aged paint and varnish darken toward this tone, so the match is a look-alike hue in an old photograph, not a pigment [7]. The painter most devoted to it is Kano Tan'yū, who has it in 12 of 14 works here [7]. Its closest company in the archive is [[taupe]], [[fawn]] and [[khaki]] territory, and it shares canvases more than chance with Jacaranda Brown and Flint Grey [7].
